chronology.event: Operação Prato first phase begins on Colares, Pará
Operation closed with official finding of no unusual phenomena
Gives interview to ufologists Ademar José Gevaerd and Marco Antônio Petit
Found dead at home approximately three months after the interview

claims.source: Wikipedia 'Operação Prato', citing ISTOÉ (22 July 2013) and Folha de S. Paulo (11 January 2009)
claims.text: 'The operation was commanded by Captain Uyrangê Bolivar Soares Nogueira de Hollanda Lima ... After approximately four months, the operation was closed after finding no unusual phenomena. The official documents can be obtained from the Brazilian National Archives (Arquivo Nacional).'

claims.source: Andy Wells, 'Operation Saucer: The Official Search For UFOs That Attacked Brazilians With Light Beams In 1977', Yahoo News
claims.text: 'Three months after giving the interview, Captain Hollanda was found dead in his home after he seemingly hung himself using the belt of his bathrobe.'

claims.source: Fernando Rodrigues, 'SNI investigou óvnis durante a ditadura', Folha de S. Paulo, 11 January 2009, pp. A10-A11
claims.text: Operação Prato was executed jointly by the Brazilian Air Force and the National Information Service (SNI), the dictatorship's intelligence agency; Folha de S. Paulo reported in January 2009 that 'SNI investigou óvnis durante a ditadura'.

conflicts.text: The Air Force's official finding was that nothing unusual was found; Hollanda's 1997 interview and the accounts of Colares residents describe injuries, burns and puncture wounds. Both cannot be true; the released Arquivo Nacional file is the arbiter and has not been fully worked in this pass.

connections.edgeLabel: Hollanda was a serving FAB officer, not a civilian investigator
connections.label: Força Aérea Brasileira / Ministério da Aeronáutica
connections.note: Uyrangê Hollanda commanded Operação Prato as a captain of the Brazilian Air Force and retired as a lieutenant colonel. Pratt's file: 'In 1997, long after he had retired as a lieutenant colonel, Hollanda decided he was no longer obligated to remain silent about Operação Prato and publicly discussed Operação Prato.' The institutional tie matters because his later account contradicts the service's official negative finding — the contradiction is internal to the FAB, not between the FAB and outsiders.

connections.note: Basterfield records that Pratt 'visited Colares for the first time in February 1979, then twice after that. He interviewed Captain Uyrange Hollanda, who had led the official investigation in the Colares region. Pratt was later able to secure brief summaries of 281 incidents in Colares and surrounding areas, plus maps, and twenty photographs.' Hollanda told him his team 'took about three hundred photos and we photographed eight different types of UFOs.' Tier 2: the interview and the 281 summaries are reported by a named researcher quoting Pratt's 1996 book, and the Pratt file at The Black Vault is the surviving public artefact of that chain.

label: Capitão Uyrangê Bolívar Soares Nogueira de Hollanda Lima
narrative: Captain Uyrangê Bolívar Soares Nogueira de Hollanda Lima commanded Operação Prato, the Brazilian Air Force operation mounted in late 1977 on the island of Colares in Pará after residents reported being injured by descending lights they called the Chupa-Chupa and the mayor, José Ildone Favacho Soeiro, formally asked the Air Force for help. The operation ran in two phases, 20 October to 11 November 1977 and 25 November to 5 December 1977, and was executed by the Brazilian Air Force with the National Information Service, the military dictatorship's intelligence agency. Photographs of lights were taken; the operation was closed after roughly four months and its official finding was that no unusual phenomena had been found. Twenty years later, in 1997, Hollanda gave an interview to the Brazilian ufologists Ademar José Gevaerd and Marco Antônio Petit in which he recounted what he and his men had lived through - an account fundamentally at odds with the official negative finding. Three months after that interview he was found dead at his home, apparently having hanged himself with the belt of his bathrobe. He is the closest thing the Brazilian record has to a custody-adjacent officer who spoke and then died, and the sequence - operation, official denial, twenty years of silence, interview, death - is the reason the case has never settled.
